title: The easy no at 400×
intro: A hospital chain screens at 400 times earnings. Your screen says skip it. Open the books before you agree.

facts.label: The multiple
facts.value: ~400× trailing earnings — among the most expensive-looking stocks in the market.

facts.label: The other multiple
facts.value: EV/EBITDA is unremarkable for a hospital chain — operating cash generation looks nothing like the P/E suggests.

facts.label: The capex decade
facts.value: Nearly ₹1,700 crore deployed: beds added, LINACs bought, new cities entered, Milann acquired. Depreciation from all of it flows through the P&L now; the earnings from it arrive later.

facts.label: The honest weakness
facts.value: Five-year median ROCE: 12% — the deployed capital has not yet earned respectable returns.

facts.label: The business
facts.value: India's largest cancer-focused hospital chain — structurally growing demand, long asset lives.

question: What does the 400× actually mean?
choices: The market has gone mad — no business is worth 400× earnings
P/E is the wrong lens here: heavy capex depresses EPS via depreciation while EBITDA is ordinary — but the 12% ROCE is a real concern the EV/EBITDA lens must not excuse
It's a bargain — high P/E always means high quality
debrief: The 400× is mostly an accounting artifact: a decade of expansion capex generates depreciation today and earnings tomorrow, so EPS is crushed exactly when the asset base is newest. EV/EBITDA reads the operations honestly. But the composition chart's second slice is the discipline: 12% median ROCE means the capital hasn't earned its keep yet — the EBITDA lens must carry that question, not bury it. The transferable rule: an absurd multiple is a prompt to find the accounting cause AND the genuine weakness — screens raise questions; only the case work answers them.
